summary: Adds a way in the Session Description Protocol to describe attributes of individual media sources inside a single media stream, such as separate RTP sources that share one session. Plain SDP could only describe whole streams, so this fills in the gap.

eli5.summary: A radio call can have many people talking on one line. This lets you attach a name tag to each speaker, instead of only labeling the whole line.

questions: describe individual rtp sources in sdp
what is the sdp ssrc attribute
how to describe multiple rtp sources in sdp
subtitle: Adds SDP attributes to describe individual RTP sources by SSRC, and to group related sources together.

tldr.problem: SDP can describe a whole media stream, but has no way to describe the individual RTP sources inside it, or to say that one endpoint will use several sources.
tldr.mechanism: A new media-level attribute, ssrc, attaches source-level attributes such as cname, previous-ssrc and fmtp to a specific SSRC. A second attribute, ssrc-group, expresses relationships among sources, with initial semantics FID and FEC.
tldr.outcome: Endpoints can signal sources and how they relate, for example original and retransmission sources. Receivers that do not understand the attributes ignore them, so senders must be prepared for that.

today: RFC 5576 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated. It is where the ssrc and ssrc-group SDP attributes and the source-level attribute registries are defined.

sections.title: The Gap in SDP
sections.content:
SDP (RFC 4566) describes multimedia sessions and the media streams in them, but offers no way to describe individual media sources within a media stream. Some protocols, notably RTP single-source multicast, had to use mechanisms specific to each protocol to describe the sources of an RTP session.

RTP (RFC 3550) allows multiple sources in one session, for example if a user has more than one camera, but SDP gave an endpoint no way to say it will use several sources. This document defines a way to describe sources by their SSRC, attach attributes to them and express relationships among them.
sections.eli5: SDP could label a whole room but not the people inside. This adds name tags for each person.

sections.title: Three Levels of Information
sections.content:
An RTP session is a group of communicating participants. The source of one stream of RTP packets is a synchronization source (SSRC), identified by a 32-bit number. SDP already has session-level information and media-level information, where a media description is the thing introduced by an m= line.

The RFC points out that the term media stream is confusing. In SDP it means a whole RTP session, while RTP uses it for a single source. Here, media stream means the SDP sense and media source means a single source of packets.

The new third level is source-level information, carried by the media-level attribute ssrc, which acts as a meta-attribute mapping source attributes to specific sources.
sections.eli5: Before there were two levels: the whole show and each stage. Now there is a third: each performer on a stage.

sections.title: The ssrc and ssrc-group Attributes
sections.content:
The form is a=ssrc:<ssrc-id> <attribute> or a=ssrc:<ssrc-id> <attribute>:<value>. The ssrc-id is the SSRC as a 32-bit unsigned integer in decimal. Lines with the same ID within a media stream describe the same source, and IDs in different media streams are not correlated. Each line carries one attribute, and for every source mentioned, the cname attribute MUST be provided. The attribute may be used for any RTP-based media transport.

The form a=ssrc-group:<semantics> <ssrc-id> ... expresses a relationship among sources, like the group attribute of RFC 3388 does for media streams. The initial semantics are FID (Flow Identification) and FEC (Forward Error Correction). A group MUST list at least one ID, and every ID MUST be defined by an ssrc: line in the same media description.
sections.eli5: Each speaker gets a number and a name tag. A group line says which speakers belong together.

sections.title: Source-Level Attributes
sections.content:
Three source-level attributes are defined. cname ties a source to the Canonical End-Point Identifier it will put in its RTCP SDES packets. It is REQUIRED whenever any source attributes are present, and MUST NOT appear more than once for the same ID in a media stream. If an SDES packet shows a different CNAME for the SSRC, the receiver SHOULD assume there has been an SSRC collision.

previous-ssrc lists earlier SSRCs for the same source after a collision forced a change, and the updated SDP MUST include it. fmtp carries format-specific parameters for one source, and its format MUST be one of the payload types of the media stream.

The RFC only defines attributes useful for decoding and rendering. Attributes that would affect accepting or rejecting a stream in offer/answer are left for future consideration.
sections.eli5: The name tag says who a speaker is. If a speaker has to change numbers, a note says what the old number was.

sections.title: Using Sources in RTP
sections.content:
SSRCs are chosen randomly by endpoints, so collisions are possible and endpoints MUST be prepared to detect and resolve them. The binding between an SSRC and a CNAME can only be confirmed from the SDES packets in the session, so SDP information may be out of date.

Endpoints MUST NOT use SSRCs mentioned in descriptions they have received for their own sources. Sources known only through SDP MUST NOT be counted for group size estimation, and report blocks MUST NOT be sent for them. Other sources can appear at any time. An endpoint whose signalled source collides with an unsignalled one MAY delay resolution by 5*1.5*Td, while collisions between two signalled sources MUST be acted on immediately.

If a signalled source changes its SSRC, the author of the SDP SHOULD send updated SDP that includes previous-ssrc, if the distribution mechanism allows updates. An SSRC ID MUST NOT be reused for the same CNAME during the participant timeout interval.
sections.eli5: Numbers are picked at random, so two people might pick the same one. The rules say who has to change and how to tell everyone.

sections.title: Offer/Answer and Compatibility
sections.content:
With the offer/answer model (RFC 3264), the attributes describe only the sources each party is willing to send. There is no way to accept or reject individual sources. If the set of sources is unacceptable, the answerer can only reject the media stream or the whole session. SSRC IDs in an answer MUST differ from those in the offer.

SDP interpreters ignore unknown attributes, so endpoints MUST be prepared for recipients that do not understand source descriptions. Some deployed RTP implementations may not support multiple media sources in a media stream, so senders MAY restrict themselves to a single source unless they know receivers support multiplexing.
sections.eli5: You can accept the whole list of speakers or refuse the whole call, but you cannot pick just some of them.

sections.title: Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives three examples. The first declares one source in an audio stream. The second shows a video stream where one participant, with a single CNAME, uses two sources, for example because of several cameras.

The third shows retransmission (RFC 4588) using SSRC multiplexing, where ssrc-group:FID lines pair each original source with its retransmission source. This avoids the complexity of working out which source is which.
sections.eli5: A group line says "these two numbers are a pair", like a player and their instant-replay camera.

sections.title: IANA and Security
sections.content:
IANA registered the media-level attributes ssrc and ssrc-group. The RFC creates a new registry, att-field (source level), seeded with cname, previous-ssrc and fmtp, and a registry of ssrc-group semantics seeded with FID and FEC. New group semantics MUST be defined in Standards Track RFCs.

On security, all the implications of RTP and SDP apply, and explicitly describing multiplexed sources does not appear to add any further security issues.
sections.eli5: There is an official list of allowed name tag types, and new ones must be added to it properly.

data.code:
m=video 49174 RTP/AVPF 96 98
a=rtpmap:96 H.264/90000
a=rtpmap:98 rtx/90000
a=fmtp:98 apt=96;rtx-time=3000
a=ssrc-group:FID 11111 22222
a=ssrc:11111 cname:user3@example.com
a=ssrc:22222 cname:user3@example.com
a=ssrc-group:FID 33333 44444
a=ssrc:33333 cname:user3@example.com
a=ssrc:44444 cname:user3@example.com

items.desc: The CNAME the source puts in its SDES packets; required.
